Over the years my focus went more and more towards multiplayer games since anything else seemed to be repetetive to an unbearable extent.

Well then along came this game.

It confronts you as the player with your own expecations to video games. Expectations that have been created by putting in countless hours into the monotonous content that so called AAA-studios feed to the communtiy.
This experience alone was enlightening and refreshing alike, whilest being allowed to whitness true creativity.

When I finally watched those end-credits it reminded me of beating Super Mario World for the first time back in 1992.
I just sat there, feeling weirdly touched by what I just went through waiting for another curveball.
Of course my expectations were too standard, again.

Inscryption is the most unusual and fun game I have experienced in many many years. It's a game that oozes with so much energy and dedication, something that I didn't think games together with the reasons behind their developement had still in it. 

Thanks and kudos go to its creators for putting a game out there that feels like true rebellion.

Inscryption is a game that both impressed and disappointed me. When I played the demo I was so excited for the full game. I preordered it (which I dont do alot on steam) and booted it up as soon as I could. What the demo did promise was ultimately delivered. There is a fun, roguelike card game that makes you think about every card you play, where you play it, and when you play it. I loved the art style and creepy atmosphere. Im a big Binding of Isaac fan and the fact that it was a roguelike where you start again just a little more powerful made me so excited to play it for possibly hundreds of hours. Inscryption is unfortunately not that kind of game.

**This next paragraph is going to contain slight narrative spoilers. No specific plot points but how the story is told. fair warning**

My disappointment started when I realized this is the kind of game where alot of the enjoyment happens is on the first playthrough of it, There is nothing to be gained from subsequent playthroughs in terms of deckbuilding or improving your characters "stats". The story being told is the main reason to play and once youve seen the story to the credits, thats it. No real reason to play again other than to experience the story after youve forgotten what happens. With that being said I still really enjoyed my roughly 12-13 hour experience. There was alot of surprises and things happening to keep you wanting to continue to see what happens next. I hope they come out with a spinoff where its basically the same card game but it focuses more on replayabilty like in the demo and the expand the gameplay further from there.

Edit: The devs released a beta for an upcoming expansion called Kaycee's Mod. This mod has took my one sole complaint about the game and fixed it. The game can now just be infinitely played without having to stop for any reason except for the sweet release of death. The mod introduces something similar to the Halo skulls where you can pick certain things to make the game more challenging for yourself only in this game you get rewarded based on your progress with the skulls activated. Apparently there are new cards to be unlocked and I could not be happier. Easy reccomendation to any roguelike fan that enjoys deckbuilding!

I implore you. If you think you might be interested in this game at all, be careful. I went in blind and that is most certainly the way to go. If you carelessly search around, watch someone play too far into the gameplay loop, or read much about it you will totally spoil what I can only call an [i]experience[/i] that you can't get back.

With that out of the way, I'm afraid I can only say that my review must be vague and shallow for the same reasons. 

Inscryption is creepy as hell, deeply stylized, dripping with atmosphere and charm, and continues to draw me in further the more I play it. Its quite a clever premise, and I suspect this 'style' might be one of the next big things that other devs attempt to copy or capture the magic of.

At its core, it certainly is a deck based card battle game with roguelike elements exactly as described on the tin. It might seem really difficult at times during the early stages but once you're familiar with the mechanics and make progress, the core gameplay loop is so very satisfying to play through. But Inscryption is so much [b]more[/b] and that's the essence of why knowing as little as possible beyond the main points is vital to enjoy it to the fullest. 

The game has already thrown quite a few surprises at me and the deeper in I go, the weirder it gets and I love that.

Its phenomenal.

The story line is a bit unique and unexpected.   First run takes about 35 hours for all contents. 

Achievements in the game are well designed.  Some of them are quite challenging.  

While the game runs perfectly on steam deck, there's one achievement that is much easier to get on PC instead.  Unfortunately there're some issues for cloud saves transfer between steam deck default version and PC version.  The solution is to use an earlier version of proton (proton 7. something) while playing on steam deck, for saving on the same cloud save slot as PC version.

Inscryption is a wholly unique experience, and I rarely say that about most games I've played, but Daniel Mullins has created something truly spectacular here. Like most, I went in expecting to play another seemingly ordinary card game. But, just like most people, I was quickly proven wrong. Inscryption is an eccentric beast of a game, one that prides itself on its rich and dense horror atmosphere and sound design, nonlinear meta storytelling as well as its addicting roguelite gameplay. In short, it's a card game unlike any other. An experience that utterly has no parallel. Trust me, my words alone cannot do it justice. Although somewhat premature of me to declare this so soon after finishing, it wouldn't surprise me if Inscryption ends up being fondly remembered and lauded by future generations of gamers, in the same vein as titles as Bioshock, as the game that helped pushed its genre forward in a brighter and more innovative direction. And frankly, I don't think there's a greater compliment a game can receive than that. For your consideration: Inscryption.

The Best of its genre. This will be a largely spoiler-free review to the best of my ability. It is a challenging game to review at any length without spoilers, but I won't put any in here. In truth, Inscryption is one of the best games ever made and is easily the number one in its genre. How the developers fused a deck-building game with psychological horror, two polar opposite genres, into one game is nothing short of something worth being universally lauded. The game starts in a cabin with a mysterious figure. You can't leave the cabin, and this figure, who acts as a sort of Dungeon Master, leads the game, and you play along. Most of the game is deck-building and playing with its unique rules. It's easy to learn, and you'll likely find it the most enjoyable part. The gameplay for the card-playing aspects is genuinely fun. Around the cabin, you've got little things to do; you can leave the table at more or less any time, and a few puzzles to solve that are worth doing and will aid you in your quest to beat the mysterious cabin figure. That being said, I'll mostly end my review here; the game only gets better the more you play it, and you'll be pleasantly surprised at what you find. The writing is phenomenal and philosophical, as well as downright sadistic. The Soundtrack is also an absolute banger. I'll recommend this game to anyone and everyone. It's genuinely some of the most fun I've had last year. 10/10. Daniel Mullins is fucking genius. Please don't wait for a sale; it's worth the full price; go and get it!

[i]Obviously, this review doesn't feature considerable spoilers.[/i]

[h3]Cabin in the Woods[/h3]
I've beaten the demo twice in anticipation, which never happened to me before. I recommend checking it out first, naturally. What can you reliably expect from the full game? An elaborate meta-narrative in the finest tradition of The Hex and Pony Island. Prepare to feel sorry for cards, experience empathy towards villains, find peace in failure, and doubt in victory. That and quite a few hours of engrossing gameplay I promise, but everything else in this story is subject to change.

It begins in a cabin in the woods where you're held hostage by Leshy who makes you play the game that uses his living cards. Leshy is a complicated creature from the Slavic mythology who, I think, got a reasonably authentic representation here. This is more or less how he looks, and what he does, or would do nowadays, also isn't that far off - beasts and mind games are definitely his field of expertise. If he reminds you of a grabby homeless man, well, this is because, most likely, some legendary hermits were at the root of the myth, to begin with.

[h3]NASCAR||Formula 1[/h3]
It's completely unique for a card game to put [i]such[/i] strong accents on its setting, characters, and atmosphere. I would cautiously compare this bold approach to gems like Ring of Pain and Hand of Fate when it comes to humor and personality. Beautiful in all of its manifestations, the goodness starts off being soaked in a bizarre, stylish, almost bleak fairy-tale atmosphere reminiscent of Darkwood. These are surface-level comparisons, a feeble image in relation to the full picture, but I don't mind - it's a firm hook.

People ask ignorant questions like "is it better than Monster Train?", and to me, it's like taking a Formula 1 bolide and saying that "it's better than a NASCAR car". I mean, they're both cars, they share a lot of elements that can be compared, right? But anyone would understand how inappropriate a direct juxtaposition of these two things is. Likewise, these games have different goals and use different means to achieve them. I, for one, always turned 180 degrees, built up speed, and then rammed into everyone in my NASCAR simulators.

[h3]"A ghastly spectacle but the soul of the wolf cub now lives in the adder."[/h3]
Inscryption is a deckbuilder where you'll be playing unlimited cards per round on a grid and sometimes examine your surrounding to solve puzzles like it's The Room. These are the only constant mechanics, the connective tissue, but I won't be going into detail. Suffice to say that I found the core card game as well as the puzzles extremely enjoyable. Besides, the game teaches you its mechanics gently and patiently, you can always click RMB to get a tip on just about anything and check the Rulebook at any time.

The enemy doesn't necessarily adhere to the exact same rules as you do and I loved how thematically coherent it is. Battles usually start with your adversary having a few cards on the board, bosses have more lives than you are allowed. So, don't expect a fair fight, it's an abusive relationship where you're a pawn doomed to sacrifice your brethren - spill their blood and conjure their bones. Leshy gets all he wants for free because he's in control. Sometimes it may seem unfair, so I've prepared a word of advice next.

The game has so much to offer, don't give up. If you think it's too hard for you early on, just pray for a milk run. The first act is the hardest part of the game, but it's balanced in a way that makes breaking it easy if you pay attention. Counter-intuitively, cannon fodder is valuable, don't dismiss weak creatures. In droves, they will be very useful on most of the bosses, including the "last" one. Bosses tend to destroy/transform/steal your first wave of troops, so best make them ants, rabbits, and bees. Finally, always go for Mantis Gods, all game long.

[h3]We've Come a Long Way, Psycho Mantis[/h3]
What happens after the first act? You have to see it to believe it, or just play enough games from this developer to already foresee something like that. And I don't mean it in a derogatory sense, this isn't some mundane ass-pulling - even when you know the twist is coming, it's gonna be a clever surprise anyway when these people do it. After Inscryption, I was left wallowing in ambivalence. I'm not so sure if I've beaten it, I'm so lost that I don't even know if I've won. And I love it! Or do I?

From now on, any game attempting something like this would have to go completely out of bounds and take serious risks to be on par. But most importantly, within all the brilliant twists and competent use of a great variety of complex meta-schemes, there lies an exceptional game that cuts above and gets you involved through its ingenious gameplay rather than by other, less relevant means. Infinitely commendable. I recommend Inscryption so hard that I almost fell from my chair while writing this.

I bought and completed this game earlier this year and recently came back to 100% it. Shockingly, when I came back, I didn't get annoyed or frustrated by any backtracking or repetition. In fact, sometimes I'd consider fighting just one more boss, or revisiting a secret room or dialogue option. This game really has a way of pulling you in. As someone who loves strategy and card games, this game was an absolute blast to play over and over again. The story and the characters are intriguing and make me excited to find out what will happen next, regardless of if I've seen it or not. I also love that the community has discovered different deck strategies and shared them (these definitely came in handy whenever I got stuck on a boss or challenge), and how you can make your own random deck using so many different strategies. The functionality of each card is very versatile, sometimes you'll get a new card and discover it's more useful than you thought!

Some possible negatives (spoiler free):

-Repetition
At the beginning, the game can be a bit repetitive, which can get frustrating (especially if you repeatedly die or miss something). Nothing sucks more than getting to a boss only to die and restart. However, there's often something that changed or a new secret that will help you have a better start on your next run. And, if it's any consolation, this mechanic is  only present in the first act. (As mentioned previously, you can also look for popular decks online that may make your life easier).
 
- Changes in Scenery Between Acts
This game is separated into three acts, all of which have their own unique charm. However, I will say Act 1 was my favourite, based on the vibes and story telling. Act 2 and Act 3 were also fun, though my enjoyment was more based on the lore rather than the gameplay. The gameplay was not bad, but it was a slight change from Act 1 that I could see deterring people from finishing the game. The change was lore significant, and because of that, I believe it is a positive addition to the game that builds more depth.


Honestly, I really adore this game and I strongly recommend it despite the negatives. I watched a full playthrough of this game a couple years ago, and while I wish I entered the game blind, it was still such an enjoyable game to play. If you enjoy card/strategy games, I highly recommend this game. Or, if you don't like card/strategy games, I recommend watching some gameplay of it and consider purchasing it because this game is still wonderful story-wise.

Act 1 is so much fun. The style the game takes on is super cool. The eeriness of the cabin, as well as who you're opposing, creates such an interesting mood. The card game itself is addicting. Although it may seem unfair when you die to a boss and have to restart, upgrading cards, discovering new ones, solving puzzles, and slowly building that extremely overpowered card make the journey feel exciting rather than sluggish. Discovering a strat to use on a boss you previously thought was just straight-up unfair is so satisfying and would give me the same rush Souls games would. The mystery behind what the hell is even happening is intriguing and keeps you wanting to play. 

...That is until you finish the relatively short first act. Which also happens to be the ONLY act you see on the store page, or anyone playing online. The second act has you play a 16-bit top-down RPG. There's still a card game, but the fundamentals have completely changed and it's just not as fun. The deck building is wonky and 80% of the cards are unplayable and will cause you to lose every encounter. The change in style made things somewhat hard to read (and just annoying) and I simply didn't care to be as involved with my deck as I did in the first act and had one randomized for me. The third act is not as bad, but it's mediocre and lost me entirely. It's a different card game from the first two, and it's just boring this time. There's no intrigue or mystery anymore. It almost feels like you're playing for nothing and the setting/mood isn't interesting. Arguably worse than the second act due to it being so unbelievably mediocre. 

I get contextually why the game changes with the story, and to be fair, it's a cool concept! It just doesn't work in this case. The story means nothing to me if the game isn't consistently fun and no amount of writing or gimmicks can make up for gameplay (IMO). I don't care how eccentric they are. It's disingenuous advertising because they want to keep a "mystique" to the game, but it really feels like it's just because they know the first act is the only one worth playing.

I find myself wishing for a mixed opinion option. I find myself angered and frustrated by what I was sold versus what I eventually got. The advertisement, demo, and what drew me in are the first part of the 3 parts to the game. The biggest issue is the game and trailer seem to hint that there's MORE to the cabin but in all actuality, if you watched anyone go over the information about the secrets in the cabin, then you've basically seen them all except for 2/3 extra things that are needed to progress the plot and then leave the cabin.

My biggest issue is that the cabin becomes short if you know what you're doing. Even ignoring the game forcing you through a few extra loops in order to have enough time pass to actually unlock certain things, (That's fun to learn there are hard limits. Although you can surpass a soft-limit if you get lucky and are good enough at understanding the mechanics) the cabin is relatively short compared to the other 2 parts of the game. And that's kind of problematic. The first part of the game is my favorite, and I argue, the best part of the game. The mechanics have the right feel, relative balance (there are a lot of unbalanced cards purposely put in there to make sure you are 100% guaranteed to progress at some point), and a very good aesthetic. The mechanic of the side deck with the squirrels is one of my favorite parts. I generally dislike card games but this deck builder scratched my itch.

But, if you've read any of the negative reviews, you then run into the big issue. I won't go into detail for spoiler reasons but the game changes twice more. The second part felt like the longest but the 3rd part was probably actually longer. The second is essentially a traditional collectable card game. You have to build your deck for the duels and it introduces a bunch of new mechanics. But the main issue for me is that lack of side deck. I have had fights be over quickly because of insanely bad draws. Some of the 4 factions just kind of suck. It's also not helped that you are literally getting 4 different mana types that all function differently compared to the cabin where you have 2, the sacrifices and the bones. The second part is a slog for me. It's not fun and has no interest to me. If the game had just been the second part, I would not have bought it or played it.

The 3rd part is a variation on the first. Although the 3rd part eventually uses a lot of the mechanics of the different factions from the 2nd part. The worst feeling though is that the cards you get just didn't interest me. The system involved what was essentially a mana system like Hearthstone, only you can increase it faster with some card effects. The 3rd part at least has the side deck and some interesting mechanics but it doesn't have some of the better deck building aspects of the first. There is no resetting your deck. It just keeps growing larger with a few minimal ways of removing cards that are not repeatable. I consider this a double edged sword. I also found the cards a lot less interesting in the 3rd part. I don't know why but the abilities just didn't draw me in. The lack of variety in your side items also didn't help me. The side items are essentially set in stone with a refresh every checkpoint. There's not the assortment you get in the 1st part. 

Funnily enough there are also 4 bosses in all 3 parts and the 1st part has the best bosses. I had to actually think about how to approach each boss and got caught on their gimmicks the first time. The second part I can't really evaluate because I just hate the system, ignoring the bosses. The 3rd part, I can comment on 3 of the bosses. One of them is laughably easy because of it's save-state type gimmick IN YOUR FAVOR. Another boss is kind of easy with how things are designed if you know your computer and where its oldest and largest files are. The final of the 4 bosses is insanely dumb. It is so RNG based that it took way too long in order to finally win it. And I only won because of someone else because of how the gimmick works. It wasn't a hard won victory. It was baffled relief that I didn't have to attempt that fight again.

Now for the story. I'm going to keep it big picture and just say that the straight story kind of made sense. At least, the plot of the characters within the game. The larger plot didn't coalesce for me. I probably missed a bunch of secret information or something. The reason I say this is because I got to the end, saw it, and then went, "Is that really how they ended this? Why?" It's not the worst ending but I saw someone ask if there were alternate endings because of just how baffling the choice they did for the "RL" plot was. I expect there will be some analysis videos by youtubers that will be required for me to even understand half of what's being hinted as happening.

End Summary: I do not want to say this is a bad game. It isn't. The problem is that it's deceptive in how it advertises itself and the best part IS the beginning. And that's my biggest issue. The beginning set up expectations and I was let down by the rest of the game.

Edit: After a second time through in order to gain the achievements I didn't get because achievements weren't fully working on launch, my opinion has stayed the same. The 2nd Act is a type of game I don't enjoy and the 3rd still has its same issues and actively sabotages you by offering you way too many cards when a small consistent deck is much more important in Act 3. Especially since there are no easy ways to remove cards if you get too many.

[h1]Introduction[/h1] 
[b]Inscryption[/b] is a collectible card game with unique mechanics mixed in with some horror elements.

[h1]Pros & Cons[/h1]
[b]Pros:[/b]
+ Unique creepy visual style
+ Great gameplay variety
+ Fun hardcode mode

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Can feel unfair at times
- Mystries are unraveled way too soon

[h1]Story[/h1]
In the dense forest devoid of any light and roamed by scary beasts, there's a wooden cabin, where you're being held prisoner. Your captor generously offers you a game of cards; the rules are simple, and the stakes are your life. 

With this simple premise, the game manages to tell a pretty interesting story. Between the rounds of playing cards, you can get up from the table and look around the cabin. Discovering all of its mysteries and figuring out a way home takes a keen eye and a sharp mind. However, after around one-third of the game most of the mysteries are unraveled and the story becomes more straightforward and less obscure. It's hard to talk about it without venturing into spoiler territory. So, I guess I'll leave it at that to not spoil your experience.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Most reviewers say that you're supposed to go into this game blind, but I respectfully disagree with this viewpoint. I won't go into detail here, just in case you might consider this a spolier. Nonetheless, it's worth noting that for the most part of the game (around 90 percent I'd say), it uses collectible card game mechanics. Which means that you have to manage a deck of cards with various abilities and make use of their combinations in order to win. So, you should be aware of it before buying the game.

If you like this type of gameplay, then you'd probably love this game. It introduces a multitude of unique mechanics, I haven't seen in other similar games. Furthermore, [b]Inscryption[/b] also mixes up its formula so often, that you always have to learn new mechanics and synergies. Since the game isn't a multiplayer one, it doesn't have to deal with the balance issues so much. Because of that you can create some heavily overpowered decks, that will mow down every opponent in just a couple of turns. After completing the game you will also unlock a hardcore mode, that focuses on the battle mechanics and really puts your deck-building skills to the test.

[h1]Graphics & Audio[/h1]
Technically the game's visuals are nothing impressive, but the low-poly style can invoke nostalgia for PS1-era games. The lighting makes a great job at hiding technical imperfections of low-poly 3D models and highlighting the most important parts, that will let your imagination fill in the blanks. The soundtrack creates a tense atmosphere, that lets you feel the high stakes of each battle. Sound effects are also top notch, interacting with the game's world gives off this strange tactile pleasure. 

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Specs: AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Laptop GPU 8GB, 32GB RAM.

The game runs at 165 FPS in 1080p at max graphical settings. There were no crashes or other technical issues with the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[b]Inscryption[/b] is an interesting take on a collectible card game genre, that can surprise even the ones who played a lot of the recent similar games. The story is also engaging even though it shows its hand way too soon. If you're a fan of card-based games or a fan of horror mysteries, I highly recommend this game.

Western Yugioh, basically, and I love it for that. Sure, as everyone has pointed out the first act is the best one, but honestly I really liked the second one - kind of what I actually wanted from a Yugioh game back in the day - and while third act is easily the weakest with regards to mechanics, I thought it was fine, and I will say I felt it made up for it in the boss fights, especially the final two. Sure, it's not a particularly deep card game and there's plenty of cheese strats you can use to trivialize otherwise challenging encounters, but this isn't Slay the Spire - it's obvious Mullins prioritized the narrative (i.e. wanted people to actually finish his game) over raw mechanics, and I for one appreciate that - not every game needs to be a 100+ hour roguelike I'll never complete, I appreciate that it's a lean 14 hour game. Sure, you could argue the writing is also at its best when you're in the Cabin - it's more mysterious, there's a sense of urgency, Leshy is really well written and genuinely unnerving when he's in control, as opposed to P03, who comes across as a more cynical and sarcastic version of the antagonist from Pony Island - but I enjoyed the whole thing. Sure, as a guy who just cba with ARGs, I would have preferred a bit more exposition about the Luke Carder / GameFuna bits in the actual game itself, but eh, I know Mullins work so I knew what I was getting into, and I'm kind of baffled by the criticisms that claim the game is somehow pretentious or trying to be smarter than it is or whatever - gimmicky, sure, but again, I knew it would be going in.
